chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali Majiluyah (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us, saying: My uncle Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim narrated to me, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah al-Barqi, from Muhammad ibn Ali al-Kufi, from Ibn Baqqah, from Zakariya ibn Muhammad, from Abdul Malik ibn Abi Umayr, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) who said:

Four [types of people] whose prayer is not accepted: the unjust Imam, the man who leads the people in prayer while they are unwilling [towards him], the fugitive slave who runs away from his masters without necessity, and the woman who leaves her husband's house without his permission.
ai.seo_question: What are the four conditions that invalidate a person's prayer according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq identifies these four categories as having specific impediments to the validity of their prayer, distinguishing between structural flaws in leadership (the unjust Imam and the unwilling congregation) and personal status issues (the runaway slave and the disobedient wife). In Shia jurisprudence, this highlights the importance of both internal sincerity and external social hierarchy in the context of communal worship, emphasizing that prayer is not merely a ritual but a reflection of one's standing and authority.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 4-94 Muhammad ibn Ali Majiluyih - may God be pleased with him - narrated that his uncle Muhammad ibn Abil-Qasim quoted Ahmad ibn Aba Abdullah al-Barqy, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Ali al-Kufy, on the authority of Ibn Biqah, on the authority of Zakaria ibn Muhammad, on the authority of Abdul Malik ibn Abi Umayr that Aba Abdullah as-Sadiq (MGB) said, “

Prayers of the following four are not accepted: an unjust leader, an unwanted leader, a fugitive slave who has run away from his master unjustly; and a woman who leaves her husband’s house without his permission.”
